prompt.en: Two nearby portable Yagis point their booms at each other, but one has upright elements and the other has level elements. Which change addresses polarization mismatch?

text.en: Rotate one antenna about its boom until the elements have the same orientation.

feedback.en: The elements set polarization. Matching them addresses the stated local line-of-sight mismatch.

text.en: Turn both booms away while keeping element orientations unchanged.

feedback.en: Changing aim does not align the electric-field orientations and may reduce directional gain.

text.en: Add an equal length of coax to both stations.

feedback.en: Cable length does not align the antennas' polarizations.

text.en: Move a feed-point balun to the radio while leaving both antennas unchanged.

feedback.en: A balun addresses a balance transition, not the mismatch between electric-field orientations.

explanation.en: For a Yagi, separate pointing direction from element orientation. Both matter on a local path.

prompt.en: Two dipoles cut to the same dimensions resonate at different frequencies after installation. One is close to metal siding. What should be investigated first?

text.en: Whether the first-cut formula guarantees identical installed resonance.

feedback.en: A first-cut estimate is not a guarantee. Nearby objects can change installed behaviour.

text.en: The effect of nearby objects and end conditions on electrical length.

feedback.en: Equal physical cuts can behave differently in different surroundings.

text.en: Whether changing coax length will necessarily make both wires physically resonant together.

feedback.en: Cable length can change the impedance seen at the radio under mismatch, but it does not guarantee equal antenna resonance.

text.en: Whether equal transmitter power forces equal resonant frequencies.

feedback.en: Operating power does not replace the length and environment factors that set resonance.

explanation.en: Keep the model limits in view when applying a wire-length estimate to real installations.

prompt.en: A calculator entry uses 300 / 0.92 to estimate wavelength at 0.92 GHz. Which repair makes the shortcut valid?

text.en: Keep the entry and label the result metres because all frequency prefixes work.

feedback.en: The 300 shortcut requires MHz. A GHz number makes the result a thousand times too large.

text.en: Multiply the result by 1 000 because GHz is a larger unit.

feedback.en: That moves the answer in the wrong direction. Higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength.

text.en: Convert to 920 MHz, then calculate 300 / 920 ≈ 0.326 m.

feedback.en: Converting GHz to MHz gives the correct input unit for this free-space shortcut.

text.en: Use 143 / 0.92 because it already includes the GHz conversion.

feedback.en: 143 is a practical dipole factor with MHz input, not a conversion for GHz.

explanation.en: Units are part of a formula. The free-space wavelength shortcut uses metres and megahertz together.
